# 1982 Los Angeles Rams–Green Bay Packers game

The 1982 Los Angeles Rams–Green Bay Packers game was a National Football League regular-season contest played on September 12, 1982, at Milwaukee County Stadium in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. It was the Week 1 opener of the strike-shortened 1982 season and the teams’ only meeting that year. The Packers defeated the Rams 35–23 after trailing 23–0 at halftime, scoring 35 unanswered points in the second half. Team publications and regional media have identified the comeback as the largest winning rally in Packers history at the time; the 23-point margin has remained a benchmark in franchise records and retrospectives. The game aired on CBS; the television broadcast featured Jack Buck and Hank Stram on commentary, as preserved on surviving recordings. Attendance was reported as 53,694. 

## Background

- Season context and format: The 1982 NFL season was interrupted by a players’ strike that began on September 21 and lasted 57 days, reducing the regular season from 16 to 9 games and leading to an expanded postseason format that admitted the top eight teams per conference regardless of division standings. Green Bay ultimately qualified and won its first playoff game since 1967 under the “Super Bowl Tournament” format. 

- Teams and coaches: The Packers were coached by Bart Starr, then in his eighth season as head coach; the Rams were coached by Ray Malavasi. The opener in Milwaukee was the clubs’ only meeting in 1982. 

- Venue and attendance: The game was played at Milwaukee County Stadium, Green Bay’s second home venue in that era. Attendance was 53,694. 

## Teams and pre-game context

- Green Bay Packers
 - Head coach: Bart Starr. 
 - Entered the game 0–0; improved to 1–0 with the win. Green Bay would finish 5–3–1 and reach the playoffs, defeating the St. Louis Cardinals 41–16 in the Wild Card round before losing to Dallas 37–26 in the Divisional round. 
 - Core offensive personnel in the game included QB Lynn Dickey, WRs James Lofton and John Jefferson, TE Paul Coffman, and RB Eddie Lee Ivery. 

- Los Angeles Rams
 - Head coach: Ray Malavasi. 
 - Entered the game 0–0; fell to 0–1 with the loss. The Rams completed the season 2–7. 
 - QB Bert Jones started for Los Angeles; the offense also featured RB Wendell Tyler, TE Mike Barber, WR Willie Miller, and K Mike Lansford. 

## Game summary

Los Angeles dominated the first half, capitalizing on Green Bay turnovers and field position to build a 23–0 lead by halftime. The Rams opened with a 4-yard rushing touchdown by Wendell Tyler and extended the margin with Mike Lansford field goals of 32, 29, and 28 yards, plus an 8-yard touchdown pass from Bert Jones to Mike Barber. Green Bay turned the ball over six times in the game (five in the first half), leading to short fields and Rams points. 

Green Bay reversed the game’s momentum in the third quarter. Lynn Dickey directed a 55-yard drive capped by a 4-yard touchdown pass to Paul Coffman, then a short field set up Eddie Lee Ivery’s 3-yard touchdown run to bring the Packers within 23–14. Early in the fourth quarter, following a missed 51-yard field goal by Lansford that would have pushed the Rams lead to 26–14, Dickey led a rapid 66-yard drive highlighted by a 50-yard completion to Coffman and finished with a 15-yard touchdown pass to James Lofton, cutting the deficit to 23–21. On the ensuing kickoff, Los Angeles fumbled; Green Bay recovered at the Rams’ 10-yard line and scored on the next play—a 10-yard Dickey-to-Coffman touchdown—to take its first lead, 28–23. A later George Cumby interception of Jones set up the clinching drive, culminating in Ivery’s 27-yard touchdown run with 3:06 remaining. Green Bay’s defense held the Rams scoreless after halftime. Team historian accounts place the go-ahead touchdown at 3:48 of the fourth quarter and the clinching score at 3:06. 

## Scoring summary

- First quarter
 - Rams — Wendell Tyler 4-yard run (Mike Lansford kick) [7–0] 
 - Rams — Mike Lansford 32-yard field goal [10–0] 

- Second quarter
 - Rams — Mike Barber 8-yard pass from Bert Jones (Lansford kick) [17–0] 
 - Rams — Mike Lansford 29-yard field goal [20–0] 
 - Rams — Mike Lansford 28-yard field goal [23–0] 

- Third quarter
 - Packers — Paul Coffman 4-yard pass from Lynn Dickey (Jan Stenerud kick) [23–7] 
 - Packers — Eddie Lee Ivery 3-yard run (Stenerud kick) [23–14] 

- Fourth quarter
 - Packers — James Lofton 15-yard pass from Dickey (Stenerud kick) [23–21] 
 - Packers — Paul Coffman 10-yard pass from Dickey (Stenerud kick) [28–23] 
 - Packers — Eddie Lee Ivery 27-yard run (Stenerud kick) [35–23] 

Quarter-by-quarter: Rams 10, 13, 0, 0 — 23; Packers 0, 0, 14, 21 — 35. 

## Statistics

- Team totals
 - First downs: Packers 22; Rams 12
 - Total net yards: Packers 377 (149 rush, 228 net pass); Rams 271 (105 rush, 166 net pass)
 - Yards per play: Packers 5.9; Rams 4.3
 - Third downs: Packers 4/8 (50%); Rams 4/16 (25%)
 - Turnovers: Packers 6 (3 interceptions, 3 lost fumbles); Rams 3 (2 interceptions, 1 lost fumble)
 - Penalties: Rams 11 for 88 yards; Packers 2 for 15 yards
 - Time of possession: Packers 30:20; Rams 29:40 

- Individual leaders (selected)
 - Packers: Lynn Dickey 17/27, 237 yards, 3 TD, 3 INT; Eddie Lee Ivery 17 rushes, 109 yards, 2 TD; John Jefferson 6 receptions, 116 yards; Paul Coffman 4 receptions, 66 yards, 2 TD; James Lofton 4 receptions, 59 yards, 1 TD; Jan Stenerud 5/5 PAT. 
 - Rams: Bert Jones 17/31, 202 yards, 1 TD, 2 INT; Wendell Tyler 14 rushes, 57 yards, 1 TD (3 receptions, 32 yards); Willie Miller 3 receptions, 78 yards; Mike Barber 1 reception, 8 yards, 1 TD; Mike Lansford 3/4 FGs (made 32, 29, 28; missed 51), 2/2 PAT. 

- Defense and special teams
 - Packers sacks (team): 4.0 (Mike Douglass, Ezra Johnson, Terry Jones, Casey Merrill 1.0 each). Interceptions: John Anderson, George Cumby. 
 - Rams sacks (team): 2.0 (Jack Youngblood, Reggie Doss 1.0 each). Interceptions: Nolan Cromwell, Carl Ekern, Rod Perry. Punt returns: LeRoy Irvin 4 for 82 yards (long 54). 

## Officiating and broadcast

- Television: The game was televised by CBS. Surviving broadcast recordings feature Jack Buck (play-by-play) and Hank Stram (analyst). 

- Radio: The Rams’ 1982 media guide lists KMPC (710 AM) in Los Angeles among the club’s radio outlets for regular-season coverage; the guide notes a Sept. 12 regular-season game “at Green Bay (Milwaukee).” 

## Aftermath and legacy

- Immediate standings: Green Bay moved to 1–0; Los Angeles fell to 0–1. 

- Season outcomes: The Packers finished 5–3–1 in the strike-shortened season, won a Wild Card playoff game over the St. Louis Cardinals 41–16, and lost 37–26 at Dallas in the Divisional round. The Rams finished 2–7. 

- Significance: Team historical accounts and later coverage have identified the 23-point rally as the largest comeback victory in Packers history, a distinction highlighted in organizational histories and media retrospectives. It has been cited in lists of notable Packers comebacks and season openers. Attendance for the game was documented at 53,694. The turnaround hinged on a string of second-half plays noted in team histories: a missed 51-yard field goal by the Rams, a go-ahead touchdown following a fumbled kickoff recovered at the Los Angeles 10-yard line, and a late interception by George Cumby preceding Eddie Lee Ivery’s clinching 27-yard touchdown run. 

## Notes on identification and scope

- Game identity and uniqueness in 1982: The September 12, 1982 contest at Milwaukee County Stadium was a Week 1 regular-season game and the only Rams–Packers meeting of the 1982 season. 

## Media coverage and reaction

Subsequent historical features by team and regional media have revisited the game as a benchmark comeback. Packers team histories have framed it as “the greatest comeback in team history,” and later Milwaukee Journal Sentinel coverage has ranked the rally among the franchise’s foremost comebacks and top season openers.

The Packers' Texas-sized comeback on Sunday matched the biggest winning rally in franchise history. The previous victory came on Sept. 12, 1982, against the Los Angeles Rams.

Here are some highlights from that game played in front of 53,694 fans at County Stadium:

■The Packers scored 35 straight points after falling behing, 23-0, in the first half.

■Green Bay had five turnovers before halftime. Quarterback Lynn Dickey played a part in four of them, throwing two interceptions and losing two fumbles.

■Dickey bounced back by completing 8-of-12 passes for 157 yards and three touchdowns in the second half. Tight end Paul Coffman caught two of the scores and James Lofton the other.

■The Packers outgained the Rams in total yards, 377-271. Eddie Lee Ivery had 109 yards rushing for Green Bay.

■Green Bay had two touchdowns in the third quarter and three in the fourth.

■The Rams didn't have a first down for the first 17 minutes of the second half.

■On the kickoff following Dickey's TD pass to Lofton, Packers special teamer Guy Prather forced a fumble from Rams returner Robert Alexander. Prather recovered the ball, setting up a Dickey-to-Coffman score that gave the Packers the lead at 28-23.

Remmel: Memorable '82 Comeback Highlights Rams Series
=====================================================

 Oct 02, 2006 at 07:00 PM

*   [](https://www.packers.com/news/remmel-memorable-82-comeback-highlights-rams-series-2452938 "Share on Facebook")
*   [](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Remmel%3a+Memorable+%2782+Comeback+Highlights+Rams+Series&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.packers.com%2Fnews%2Fremmel-memorable-82-comeback-highlights-rams-series-2452938 "Share on Twitter")

![Image 3: 061003dickey_lynn215.jpg](https://static.clubs.nfl.com/image/private/t_editorial_landscape_mobile/f_auto/packers/fw5znhmgdaillhys8ltu.jpg)

As every card-carrying Packers aficionado well knows, Green Bay is the most titled team in the National Football League, with a dozen championships in hand.

In keeping with that imposing record, they also have a leg up on most of their rivals in their respective all-time series from the won-and-lost perspective...also known

as the bottom line.

The [St. Louis Rams](http://www.stlouisrams.com/), the opponents at hand, however, are a notable exception to the "rule."

The Rams, who will be displaying their current wares in Lambeau Field Sunday afternoon, lead the all-time rivalry, having won 44 games - four more than the Packers - in a series that dates back to 1937, when Sunday's invaders were in their original home and known as the Cleveland Rams.

To the Packers' understandable chagrin, the Rams also own the distinction of having dealt the Green and Gold the most decisive defeat in their postseason history - a 45-17 verdict forged in a dismal playoff at St. Louis on Jan. 20, 2002.

It was an indignity accentuated by the Missourians' larcenous defense, which intercepted six Brett Favre passes to accelerate the humbling process.

Fortunately, in turn, the Packers have had some singular moments against the Rams, chief among them their 28-7 Western Conference playoff victory at Milwaukee County Stadium in December of 1967 - eight days prior to what became the legendary "Ice Bowl" triumph over the [Dallas Cowboys](http://www.dallascowboys.com/).

And, beyond that memorable success, it was against the Rams that the Packers also enjoyed the greatest comeback in their long and distinguished annals.

Historically, it was to become a major highlight in the coaching career of Bart Starr, then in the eighth season of his nine-year tenure as head coach of the Packers.

The scene was Milwukee County Stadium and it was opening day of the 1982 NFL season (Sept. 12).

The Rams, with Bert Jones presiding at quarterback, moved out to a 23-0 halftime lead with the aid of three field goals by placekicker Mike Lansford as Los Angeles capitalized on a like number of Green Bay turnovers.

As the teams departed the field for their respective locker rooms at the intermission, the Packers were not aware that no Green Bay team trailing by as many as 23 points at halftime ever had come from behind to win a game.

Whatever the case, the substantial deficit had no apparent effect upon quarterback Lynn Dickey, who rebounded from an unsteady start to direct a remarkable second-half reversal - one punctuated by five touchdowns and 35 unanswered points en route to an astonishing 35-23 victory.

It was a tribute, in large part, to a suddenly tightfisted defense, which not only blanked the Rams over those last 30 minutes but held them to an exceedingly modest four first downs in the smothering process.

The second half renaissance began innocuously enough when, early in the third quarter, Dickey capped a 55-yard drive with a 4-yard scoring pass up the middle to tight end Paul Coffman. Following the first of Jan Stenerud's five conversions, the Packers still trailed the Rams, 23-7.

But not for long. Quickly forcing a punt after the subsequent kickoff, they were back in the end zone just three plays later.

Fullback Mike Meade launched the "drive" routinely with a 2-yard gain over right guard, after which Dickey promptly found Coffman with a 42-yard strike to the Rams' 3-yard line.

Running back Eddie Lee Ivery finished the project on the very next play, bolting off right tackle into the end zone.

The unfolding comeback was temporarily interrupted by Nolan Cromwell's interception of a Dickey pass near midfield, but the Rams shortly went empty-handed when a 51-yard Lansford field goal attempt veered wide left early in the fourth quarter.

The Packers continued their burgeoning resurgence, moving 66 yards in four plays to their third touchdown, 50 of them coming on a Dickey "bomb" to Coffman. Dickey then completed the process with a 15-yard strike to wideout James Lofton, then already well on his way to the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

The football fates then smiled warmly upon the Green and Gold.

Rams kickoff returner Kermit Alexander fumbled the succeeding kickoff, which was promptly recovered by Packers linebacker Guy Prather at the Los Angeles 10-yard line.

Whereupon Dickey took advantage with alacrity, firing a 10-yard bullseye to Coffman, who registered his second touchdown of the afternoon and propelled the Packers into their first lead of the day, 27-23.

A George Cumby interception at the Green Bay 30 then enabled the Packers to complete the comeback late in the fourth quarter. Meade's 19-yard burst up the middle, complemented by a 5-yard face mask penalty, was the key maneuver en route.

Two plays later, the artful Ivery slipped through the middle on a well-executed "draw" and cantered 27 yards to the game's final touchdown.

Stenerud added the 35th and final point of the record comeback with 3:06 remaining.

*Continuing an association with the team that is more than 55 years old, [Lee Remmel](https://www.packers.com/news/remmel-memorable-82-comeback-highlights-rams-series-2452938) was [named the first official Team Historian](https://www.packers.com/news-and-events/article-1/packers-name-lee-remmel-team-historian/9eb331e1-5aa4-11df-a3b6-528cc843f916) of the Green Bay Packers in February 2004. The former Green Bay Press-Gazette reporter and Packers public relations director, Remmel will write regular columns for Packers.com as part of his new assignment.

In addition to those articles, Remmel will answer fan questions in a monthly Q&A column. To submit a question to Remmel, [click here.](https://www.packers.com/news/ask_lee_remmel/)*

![Image 3: 041005dickey_a.jpg](https://static.clubs.nfl.com/image/private/t_editorial_landscape_mobile/f_auto/packers/nbh0l1iq25edeabhos99.jpg)

_GREATEST COMEBACK IN PACKERS HISTORY, KEY WESTERN CONFERENCE PLAYOFF HIGHLIGHT 7-DECADE SERIES WITH RAMS_

The Packers and the [St. Louis Rams](http://www.stlouisrams.com/), who will make mutual history next week when they meet on the "Monday Night Football" showcase for the first time, have forged more than a few historic adventures over the course of their seven-decade "association."

Curiously, two of the most memorable occurred in Milwaukee - at County Stadium, the Packers' second home from 1953-1994, which since has fallen to the wrecking ball.

Chief among them, without question, was a critical 28-7 victory over the Rams in a 1967 Western Conference playoff which propelled the Packers into the fabled "Ice Bowl" against the [Dallas Cowboys](http://www.dallascowboys.com/), played in Lambeau Field just eight days later.

Close behind, from the historical perspective, was a salutary happening on Sept. 12, 1982.

The Green and Gold, down 23-0 at halftime, proceeded to execute the most dramatic comeback in team annals, erupting for 35 consecutive unanswered points in the second half to depart County Stadium with a 35-23 victory.

From the overall standpoint, the Packers dominated the early years of the series, launched in 1937 when the Rams were based in Cleveland, winning 12 and tying one of the first 14 games (they also have won five of the last seven meetings). But the Rams caught up during the '50s and today lead the series, having won 44 games to the Packers' 39.

There also have been two ties - the most recent a 24-24 standoff at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum in 1964 (the Rams became the NFL's first West Coast team when they moved to Los Angeles in 1946).

In addition, there recently has been a second playoff game, a divisional showdown in which the Rams posted a 45-17 victory at St. Louis on Jan. 20, 2002 (The Rams had moved to St. Louis in 1995).

The '67 playoff contest matched the Packers, champions of the NFL's Central Division (9-4-1) and the Rams, the Coastal Division champions (11-1-2), to determine the winner of the Western Conference title. The survivors would advance to the NFL Championship Game against Dallas in what became the "Ice Bowl."

On that occasion, things were more than somewhat chancy for the Packers in the early going, which saw the Rams move out to a 7-0 first quarter lead by way of a 29-yard Roman Gabriel scoring pass to Bernie Casey.

To compound the problem, the Rams again threatened to score early in the second quarter when defensive back Chuck Lamson waylaid a Bart Starr pass and returned it to Green Bay's 10-yard-line.

Fortuitously, premier pass rusher Henry Jordan sacked Gabriel for a 7-yard loss on third down, forcing Los Angeles to attempt a field goal by Bruce Gossett, an effort which was blocked by linebacker Dave Robinson.

One exchange later, rookie running back Travis Williams, who had become a sensation at mid-season, broke into the open over the right side and streaked 46 yards to the end zone, Don Chandler adding the extra point to tie the score at 7.

The Rams also came up empty on their next possession, Gossett's 46-yard field goal attempt falling short, and the Packers' Willie Wood staked the Green and Gold to prime field position, returning the failed kick 44 yards to the Green Bay 45.

From there, Starr had the Packers in the end zone in 7 plays, firing a 17-yard, third-down strike to wide receiver Carroll Dale for the score. Chandler's conversion made it 14-7 at the intermission.

Taking over the game in the second half, the Packers scored on a 4-yard run by running back Chuck Mercein in the third quarter and a 2-yard run by Williams in the fourth quarter while a tightfisted defense continued to hold the Rams scoreless the rest of the way.

One of the most significant victories in team annals, it set the stage for the Packers to make NFL history by becoming the only team to win three consecutive league championships since the advent of the playoff system in 1933 by defeating the Cowboys for the '67 title in the "Ice Bowl," 21-17.

Behind the scenes, the scheduling of the back-to-back post-season contests spoke volumes about Lombardi's confidence in himself and his football team. As the Packers' general manager, he had assigned the first playoff to Milwaukee, sure in his own mind that the Green and Gold would be in the NFL Championship Game - in Green Bay - eight days later.

The subsequent "comeback classic" in '82 was much like two very different games, with the Rams converting three first half turnovers into 13 points en route to that 23-0 intermission lead.

Overall, two lost fumbles and two Rams interceptions contributed substantially to the Packers' scoreless state at halftime, a point at which they had a modest 66 net yards to show for their efforts.

But things were dramatically different in the second half. Quarterback Lynn Dickey began to hit his receivers with admirable frequency and the defense collaborated by restricting the Rams to "three-and-out" on their first two third-quarter possessions.

After the first such defensive intervention, Dickey guided the Packers 55 yards to their first touchdown of the afternoon, hitting tight end Paul Coffman with a 4-yard strike for the score.

The Green and Gold were even more expeditious on the second possession of the period, winging 47 yards in three plays for the touchdown, set up by Dickey's 42-yard "bomb" to Coffman, which positioned the Packers at the 3-yard line. From there, halfback Eddie Lee Ivery burst into the end zone over right tackle on the next play. And. after Jan Stenerud's second conversion, it was a more reassuring 23-14, but still a long way to go.

A series of four "three-and-outs," two by each team, and a third Dickey interception subsequently intervened before the Packers engineered a decisive breakthrough early in the fourth quarter.

Taking over at their own 34 after Rams placekicker Mike Lansford 's 51-yard field goal attempt veered wide left, Dickey had the home forces in the end zone in four plays, the score coming on a 15-yard pass to wide receiver James Lofton. Stenerud's conversion pared the Rams' lead to two points, 23-21.

Then, right on the heels of that highly favorable development, Rams returner Kermit Alexander fumbled the succeeding kickoff and the Packers' Guy Prather recovered at the Los Angeles 10-yard line.

Dickey needed only one play from there, finding Coffman in the heart of the end zone for the score and sending the Packers into the lead for the first time at the 3:48 mark of the final period.

The suddenly embattled Rams responded with a pair of first downs following the next kickoff but an 8-yard Mike Butler sack of L.A. quarterback Bert Jones stalled the drive.

One exchange later, Packers linebacker George Cumby intercepted a Jones pass and the Packers promptly set about the finishing touches.

Ivery opened the 66-yard drive modestly enough with a 2-yard gain, after which Dickey hit Coffman with a 10-yard pass and running back Mike Meade broke through the middle for a 19-yard advance, "improved" by a 5-yard face mask penalty on the Rams.

Meade next hit left tackle for 3 yards, setting the stage for Ivery to bolt up the middle on a 27-yard draw for the game's final touchdown with 3:06 remaining in the game.

Stenerud then added the Packers' 35th consecutive, unanswered point with his fifth conversion, completing the most remarkable comeback in team annals.

_Continuing an association with the team that is more than 55 years old, Lee Remmel was [named the first official Team Historian](https://www.packers.com/news-and-events/article-1/packers-name-lee-remmel-team-historian/9eb331e1-5aa4-11df-a3b6-528cc843f916) of the Green Bay Packers in February 2004. The former *Green Bay Press-Gazette_ reporter and Packers public relations director, Remmel will write regular columns for Packers.com as part of his new assignment.

In addition to those articles, Remmel will answer fan questions in a monthly Q&A column. To submit a question to Remmel, [click here](https://www.packers.com/fans/ask/lee_remmel/). *

6.content:
There's been no shortage of impressive comebacks in the storied history of the Green Bay Packers.

A week after the "Miracle in Motown," Packer Plus reviews the top games in which Green Bay overcame the most points to emerge victorious.

### 5\. 18 POINTS vs. DETROIT

_Oct. 17, 1965; Tiger Stadium_

Trailing 21-3 at halftime, it appeared the Packers' four-game season-opening victory streak was in jeopardy. But the Lions never scored again, and Green Bay scored 28 unanswered points.

Bart Starr, who threw for 301 yards, tossed long scoring passes to Bob Long (62 yards), Tom Moore (31 yards) and Carroll Dale (77 yards) in the third quarter to take a 24-21 lead.

Fittingly, Starr finished off the scoring with a 4-yard touchdown rush in the fourth quarter. The Green Bay defense recorded three interceptions to fuel the comeback. The Packers won, 31-21.

### 4\. 20 POINTS vs. DETROIT

_Dec. 3, 2015; Ford Field_

It's a Rodgers-to-Rodgers "Hail Mary" that will go down in team lore.

Green Bay looked lethargic and lost in the first half, trailing 17-0 and 20-0 with 8:54 left in the third quarter. Sparked by Randall Cobb's recovery of James Starks' fumble in the end zone a series later, the defense created another opportunity when linebacker Julius Peppers stripped the ball from quarterback Matthew Stafford and rookie linebacker Jake Ryan recovered at the Lions 12.

Four plays later, quarterback Aaron Rodgers hit receiver Davante Adams with an 8-yard pass to trail, 20-14. Detroit tallied a 42-yard field goal early in the fourth quarter, but Rodgers responded with a 17-yard touchdown run out of a passing formation.

Trailing, 23-21, after a defensive stop, Green Bay's offense got the ball back with 23 seconds left. Facing third-and-10 following a pair of incompletions, Rodgers threw a 19-yard pass to receiver James Jones, who lateraled to tight end Richard Rodgers, who then made a final lateral to his quarterback. Aaron Rodgers was tackled for no gain by defensive end Devin Taylor as time rolled off the clock, but Taylor was flagged for a face-mask penalty.

Given one last play due to the penalty, Rodgers lofted a perfect spiral that traveled 66 yards to the end zone and was grabbed by Richard Rodgers for an improbable 27-23 victory.

### 3\. 21 POINTS vs. NEW ORLEANS

_Sept. 17, 1989; Lambeau Field_

In a 10-6 season that featured six victories by three points or less, Green Bay earned the nicknamed of the "Cardiac Pack."

After a disappointing 23-21 loss in the season opener to Tampa Bay at home, the Packers rallied from 21 down for a wild, 35-34, victory over the Saints.

New Orleans bolted out to a 21-0 lead early in the second quarter before Green Bay got on the board with Brent Fullwood's 1-yard touchdown plunge.

The Saints responded with a 38-yard Morten Anderson field goal for a 24-7 cushion at intermission.

The Packers scored two touchdowns in the third quarter to close within 24-21, but New Orleans made it 31-21 on quarterback Bobby Hebert's third touchdown pass early in the final stanza.

Quarterback Don Majkowski, who threw for 354 yards and at one point completed 18 consecutive passes, threw two touchdown passes in between another Anderson field to pull out the victory. The game-winner was a 3-yard strike to Sterling Sharpe with 1:26 left to cap an 80-yard drive in just two minutes.

### 2\. 23 POINTS vs. L.A. RAMS

_Sept. 12, 1982; Milwaukee County Stadium_

In the 1982 season opener, the Rams exploded to a 23-0 halftime lead as Los Angeles capitalized on five Green Bay giveaways.

Wendell Tyler's 4-yard rushing touchdown and Bert Jones' 8-yard scoring toss to Mike Barber along with three Mike Lansford field goals (32, 29 and 28 yards) stunned the Packers and a County Stadium crowd of 53,694.

"The Rams were on fire and we couldn't get anything going in the first half," quarterback Lynn Dickey said in a 2010 Packer Plus interview. "Then we got going."

That's an understatement.

Green Bay scored 35 points in the second half to claim a 35-23 victory. The comeback began in the third quarter with Dickey's 4-yard touchdown pass to tight end Paul Coffman, which was followed by Eddie Lee Ivery's 3-yard touchdown dash to cut the margin to 23-14.

In the fourth quarter, Dickey connected with James Lofton from 15 yards to close with 23-21 and then gave the Packers a 28-23 lead with a 10-yard touchdown strike to Coffman. Ivery completed the scoring with a 27-yard touchdown burst.

### 1\. 23 POINTS vs. DALLAS

_Dec. 15, 2013; AT&T Stadium_

This one garners the top ranking as the comeback was engineered by a backup quarterback.

In Matt Flynn's third of four starts in place of the injured Rodgers, he led a Packers comeback for the ages.

Down, 26-3, at intermission, Flynn rallied Green Bay with four second-half touchdown passes as Dallas quarterback Tony Romo tossed two interceptions in the final three minutes.

The game was tied 3-3 midway through the first quarter, but Dallas reeled off 23 consecutive points: three field goals, Romo's 25-yard touchdown pass to Jason Whitten, and DeMarco Murray's 1-yard touchdown plunge. Murray, who totaled 134 yards on 18 carries, was a huge force with a 7.4 yard-per-rush average.

Flynn started the turnaround with two third-quarter touchdown passes (13, 3 yards) sandwiching another Cowboys field goal to cut the deficit to 29-17 entering the final stanza.

With Dallas inexplicably choosing to mostly throw the ball instead of handing it off to Murray and milk the clock, Green Bay closed to within 29-24 on Flynn's 11-yard touchdown pass to James Starks.

The Cowboys pushed it to 36-24 on Romo's 5-yard touchdown pass to Dez Bryant, but the Packers responded with Flynn's 3-yard scoring aerial to James Jones to make it 36-31 with 4:17 remaining.

Dallas was driving when Romo threw a pass behind Miles Austin that was intercepted by cornerback Sam Shields at midfield. Workhorse Eddie Lacy, who gashed the Cowboys for 141 yards on 21 carries, scored from 1 yard with 1:31 left to cap the 37-36 victory.

The 2-point conversion pass failed, but Tramon Williams sealed the victory with a diving interception of Romo.

_This story appeared in Packer Plus Magazine. To subscribe, call 414-224-2222 or go to [www.jsonline.com/subscribe](http://www.jsonline.com/subscribe)._

4GEORGIA FRONTIERE President The offseason of 1982 was an active and positive time for Rams owner Georgia Frontiere. Not only did she support her coach, Ray Malavasi, but she also helped him by trading for a star quarterback in the person of Bert Jones, formerly of the Baltimore Colts. This was just one move of a busy offseason in which she worked diligently to restore the winning tradition to her Rams, who had been to the playoffs eight straight seasons until last year. Selected as a "Headliner of the Year” last spring by the Greater Los Angeles Press Club, Georgia Frontiere's activities the last four years have included all that goes into the running of a professional football franchise. Beginning with her first season, 1979, the Rams continued to prosper and win football games. That year the team went all the way to the Super Bowl and the following season it won 11 and lost five to win a spot in the NFC playoffs for the eighth straight time. In addition to running her football team, Mrs. Frontiere has found time to involve herself in numerous civic, community and charitable activities. She has been active in local youth programs, serving on the board of directors of the Los Angeles Boys and Girls Club, the Los Angeles Orphanage Guild, the Los Angeles Blind Youth Foundation, honorary vice-chairman of the Good Scout Luncheon in Orange County and co-chairman of the Boy Scout Sports Dinner in Los Angeles. DON KLOSTERMAN Assistant to the President/Consultant A key advisor to owner Georgia Frontiere, Don Klosterman enters his 11th year with the Rams after coming to the club from Baltimore with the late Carroll Rosenbloom in 1972. Born in Lemars, Iowa, Don grew up in Compton, Ca,, and attended Loyola University."The Duke of Del Rey" led the Lions through their most successful athletic era as he set seven NCAA passing records. He played pro ball with Cleveland, the Dal las Texans, the Rams and the Calgary Stampeeders before a skiing accident ended his career in 1957. Don began his front office pro football career in 1960 as a scout with the Los Angeles Chargers. He moved on to the Dallas Texans (now the Kansas City Chiefs) where he helped turn the Chiefs into a Super Bowl winner. Klosterman then became general manager of the Houston Oilers in 1966. He moved on to Baltimore as general manager in 1970, then to Los Angeles when Rosenbloom traded his Colts for the Rams, Klosterman and wife Luciana reside in Beverly Hills, Ca. He has two children, Kurt and Katie. 5^Rnms EKEtUTIUES 

JOHN SHAW Vice President-Finance John Shaw assumed the duty of vice president-finance this spring after serving the past year as the club’s secretary/treasurer. Shaw joined the club in 1980 as controller/treasurer. Before joining the Rams, Shaw spent three years with the accounting firm of Arthur Andersen & Co. A key member of the Rams organization, Shaw advises owner Georgia Frontiere on financial matters, including club investments, player contracts and legal affairs. Born In Brooklyn, N.Y., on Sept. 10. 1951, Shaw attended Kearney High School in San Diego, Ca. He went to the University of San Diego where he earned a degree in accounting in 1973. Shaw continued his education at New York University, and earned a law degree from that institution in 1976, He practiced law in Bakersfield, Ca., before joining Arthur Andersen & Co. John and wife Suzanne live in Brentwood. Ca. JACK FAULKNER Administrator of Football Operations Jack Faulkner joined the Rams'front office in 1980 after 30 years of coaching and scouting football, the previous nine years with the Rams. His duties include assisting in evaluation and signing of players, along with providing input for trades. Faulkner, born April 4, 1926, in Youngstown, Ohio, was a linebacker at Miami, Ohio, from 1946-48 after a tour in the Marine Corps (1944-45). He coached six years at the University of Cincinnati (1949-54) under Sid Gillman. then accompanied Gillman as defensive backfield coach when they joined the Rams in 1955. When Gillman left the head coaching position of the Rams fora similar spot with the Los Angeles Chargers of the AFL, Faulkner went along. He also coached for Gillman with the San Diego Chargers in 1961 before going to Denver where he remained until midway in the 1964 season, Faulkner was named AFL Coach of the Year in 1962 when he led the Denver B roncos toa7-7 record inhisfirstseasonashead coach and general manager after the team had gone 4-9-1 the previous year. In 1965 he became defensive backfield coach of the Minnesota Vikings, returning to Los Angeles in 1966 as a scout. He left to join the expansion New Orleans Saints from 1967 through 1970, serving as chief defensive coach for three years and director of player personnel the final year. 6Faulkner rejoined the Rams as a scout {1971-72), then joined the coaching staff where he remained through the 1979 season. Jack and wife Betty have a daughter, Cathy, and a son, Jonn. They live in Palos Verdes, Ca. LES MARSHALL Director of Marketing Although histitle is director of marketing, Les Marshall is also involved in many other areas of the Rams operation as he acts as a liaison between Georgia Frontiere and other staff members-Marshall joined the Rams in November, 1981, after a lengthy career with Playboy Enterprises, Inc. Marshall was employed by Playboy beginning in 1971 as Executive Assistant to the Chairman. From 1976 through 1978 he also served as President of Playboy Models and President of Playboy Limousine Co. From 1979 through 1981 he was Director of Home Video Playboy. Born on Oct. 15, 1944, at Schofield Barracks, Hawaii, Marshall attended Apple Valley (Ca.) High and Stanford University, graduating in 1966 with a degree in business. In 1976 he earned his master’s degree in business administration from Pepperdine. A former professional baseball pitcher in the Milwaukee farm system, Marshall served in Vietnam as infantry platoon leader and company commander from 1968 through 1970. He and wife Janice live in Chatsworth, Ca. DICK BEAM Director of Operations When Dick Beam agreed to accept the position of director of operations from President Georgia Frontiere, it marked a homecoming for the 44-year-old former star athlete from nearby Whittier. Beam assumed his current duties in April, 1981, and most recently held a similar position — director of admin istration — with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Beam was born May 16, 1936, in Long Beach, Ca., and graduated in 1954 from Whittier(Ca.) High, where he was a varsity letter winner in football, basketball and baseball. As a senior split end, he made prep All-America and All-CIF. He then moved on to Whittier College where he played under George Allen and Don Coryell and was an all-league performer in 1958. After graduating in 1959, Beam began a coaching career as an assistant to Coryell at Whittier before moving on as an assistant coach at Santa Fe High in 1960. He spent six seasons as an assistant at Montebello High (1961-66) before becoming head coach at Brea High in 1967 and Alhambra in 1968-71. From there he was hired by John McKay as an assistant at USC in 1972, the year the Trojans won the national championship. He worked with the defense 7that season, then moved over to offense the next three years before joining McKay in Tampa Bay in 1976. At Tampa. Beam spent a year as administrative assistant to McKay, then became director of administration in 1977, Several years ago Beam took up long distance running, and has since competed in several marathon races. He and wife Dorothy have a son, Donn, and a daughter, Cathy. They live in Dana Point. Ca. RAY MALAVASI Head Coach It was a disappointing year. 1981, but Rams Head Coach Ray Malavasi feels there is reason for optimism in 1982. For one thing, it will be the first time in his four-year career as head man in Los Angeles that he has been able to hand pick his own coaching staff. Five assistants from last year's 6-10 team have departed and Malavasi has replaced them with football men who share his philosophies. Also. Malavasi is hoping to field a healthier team in '82, particularly in the offensive line where injuries stymied his usually explosive attack last year. Losing was a new experience for Malavasi. In his three previous years as Rams head coach his teams had averaged nearly 11 wins a season, going 12-4 his first year, 9-7 in 1979 and 11-5 in 1980. The 1979 Rams beat Dallas and Tampa Bay in the playoffs to win the first NFC title in the club’s history and advance to the Super Bowl, where they gave Pittsburgh all it could handle before losing, 31-19. Whether his team is having a good season or a bad season, Malavasi is known around the league as an innovative coach. While he spent most of his time the last three years working with the team's offense, he plans to work equally with the defense in 1982. The is good news to those who like defensive football, for It was on defense that this man earned his reputation. As defensive coordinator under Chuck Knox for five years from 1973 through 1977, Malavasi guided the Rams to the defensive league leadership in several categories, including total defense, rushing defense (twice) and in scoring defense (twice). However, Malavasi has spent nearly half of his 27 years designing offenses, so it was not surprising when he was named offensive coordinator at the beginning of the 1978 season. Born Nov. 8, 1930, in Passaic, N.J., Malavasi attended Clifton High, then went on to West Point, where he studied engineeringand was a lineman under Earl (Red) Blaik and Vince Lombardi. Later he was drafted on the sixth round by the Philadelphia Eagles, but elected instead to finish his schooling at Mississippi State where he obtained a degree in civil and structural engineering and coached the freshman football team. He was commissioned in the U.S. Army as a second lieutenant and went on active duty at Fort Belvoir, Va., where, as a player-coach, one of his football teams won a service championship. Then he began an extensive collegiate coaching career, serving as an assistant at Minnesota (1956-57). Memphis State (1958-60) and Wake Forest (1961). He became personnel director of the Denver Broncos in 1962 and in 1963 became that club's defensive line coach. 9In 1966, Malavasi was name the Broncos’ interim head coach,replacing Mac Speedie, who had resigned two games into the season. Malavasi compiled a 4-8 record that year before moving on to the Canadian Football League where in 1967-68 he was defensive coach of the Hamilton Tiger-Cats. He handled the same job with the Buffalo Bills in 1969-70, then served as the Oakland Raiders’ linebacker coach in 1971-72. He became L.A.’s defensive coordinator in 1973. Ray (Raymondo Guiseppi Giovanni Baptiste Malavasi) is married to the former Mary Fleming. They have five children: Maureen, Sheila, Dennis, Bill and Bryce. Ray belongs to the St. Simon Judes Mens Club in Huntington Beach. He also served as chairman of the American Diabetes Association Celebrity Golf Classic and was active in fund raising for La Casa to benefit abused children. This summer he was named recipient of the coveted National Eagle Scout award.

## 1937 On Feb. 13, the National Football League grants a Cleveland franchise to Homer Marshman and associates,a prominent group of local businessmen. Hugo Bezdek is named head coach. As the league's rookie franchise, Rams finish with a 1-10-0 record. Bob Kelley is named radio play-by-play announcer at start of season. named club secretary. Team finishes 5-6-0. 

## 1943 Clark resigns. Chile Walsh is named head coach, but NFL grants Rams permission to suspend opera tions for one season because of war time difficulties. Reeves buys out Levy. 

## 1944 ChileWalsh becomes general manager and appoints Buff Donelli as head coach. Pickup team finishes 4-6-0. 

## 1938 Assistant coach Art Lewis takes over team after three losses and Rams win three of remaining seven games. 

## 1945 Donelli joins military service. Walsh names his brother, Adam Walsh, as head coach, with George Trafton and Bob Snyder as assistants. Third round draft choice (a future) Bob Waterfield from UCLA joins team as T-formation quarterback and leads Rams to 9-1-0 season for first divi sional title in team’s history. On icy field, Rams defeat Washington Red skins, 15-14, at Cleveland for world title. Waterfield becomes first player to receive unanimous vote for official NFL Most Valuable Player award. Walsh is named coach of the year. Eddie Kotal joins team as chief scout and Bill John begins 29-year tenure as business manager. 

## 1946 Reeves moves franchise to Los Angeles early in the year. After disappointing 6-4-1 season, both Walshes resign. 

## 1947 Reeves assumes duties of general manager. Bob Snyder is named head coach with Joe Stydahar as new assistant. Team is talent-heavy but injury-ridden in 6-6-0 season. 

## 1939 Earl "Dutch" Clark becomes head coach and Lewis remains as assistant. Rams hit .500 mark for first time with 5-5-1 record. Parker Hall joins team as rookie tailback. Hall is not named on official NFL all-league first team, but wins Joe Carr Trophy as NFL's official Most Valuable Player. 

## 1940 Team drops back to 4-6-1 record. Johnny Drake, powerful Ram fullback, is named to first team All-NFL. 

## 1941 Daniel F. Reeves and Fred Levy, Jr. purchase Rams in June and hire, as general manager, Billy Evans, former sports columnist, American League umpire and Cleveland Indians general manager. Team wins first two games but drops next nine to finish in cellar. 

## 1942 Evans resigns before 1942 season. Charles "Chile" Walsh re places Art Lewis as assistant coach. Lt. Reeves and Major Levy depart to enter armed forces. Bob Kelley is 89 Reeves sells part interests to former partner Levy and to Edwin and Harold Pauley and Hal Seley. signs. He is replaced as head coach by Hamp Pool. Team loses two of next three, but wins last eight to tie for conference title. Rams lose playoff in Detroit. Rams trade 11 players to Dallas for rookie Les Richter, who then enters Army for two years. Waterfield retires. 

## 1948 Cla rk Shaughnessy joins staff as advisory coach. On Sept. 3, Snyder resigns and Clark Shaugh nessy becomes head coach. Team wins four of last five to post 6-5-1 mark. 1953 Clubco-ownerHarold Pauley passes away. Team compiles 8-3-1 record, losing three games by total of eight points to finish third in con ference. Rams defeat world champ Lions in both games. 

## 1954 Bonus choice Bill Wade and tradee Les Richter both join Rams as rookies two years after going from college into military service. Team has disappointing 6-5-1 mark. All assistant coaches resign. Pool soon follows suit. 

## 1949 Team wins first six games, then hangs on to win first divisional title since moving west. Heavy rain holds down L.A, crowd as Philadel phia Eagles skid to 14-0 win over Rams in NFL title game. Rookie Norm Van Brocklin joins team and gives Rams top-notch one-two quarter back punch. Elroy Hirsch has fine rookie year. 

## 1950 NFL absorbs AAC, leaving Rams as lone pro team in Los Angeles after four years of two-league exis tence. In February, Stydahar becomes head coach, replacing Shaughnessy. Club opens new offices on Beverly Boulevard. Bill Granholm begins 18-year tenure as equipment manager. Team sets 22 league records in rolling to conference title tie. Water-field and end Tom Fears lead playoff win over Bears, 24-14, but following week in Cleveland, Lou Groza’s late field goal stops Rams' title hopes, 30-28. 

## 1955 On Jan. 26, Rams hire Sid Gillman, head coach at University of Cincinnati, to replace Pool. Fine de fensive year and clutch field goal kicking by Richter give team hard-fought 8-3-1 record for conference title. Cleveland wins title game at Coliseum by one-sided score. 

## 1956 In form reversal, team loses five consecutive early-season games and finishes in cellar tie with 4-8 record. 

## 1951 Rams win third straight con ference title on final day of season, then defeat Cleveland at the Coli seum, 24-17, on 73-yard pass. Van Brocklin to Fears, for first world title since moving to L.A. 

## 1957 Ram owners sign five-year operational pact and name former Ram publicist Pete Rozelleas general manager. Team loses squeakers on road to 49ers and Lions, finishing 6-6-0, but only two games behind con ference leaders. 

## 1952 Afterteam losesthree straight presason games and drops league opener by big score, Stydahar re-

## 1958 In preseason trade. Van Brocklin goes to Eagles. Bill Wade 90 sets many Ram passing marks en route to 8-4-0 year. 

## 1959 Team has general letdown and many injuries for worst season since 1937, finishing 2-10-0. Ollie Matson, acquired in big trade, is work horse at fullback. On last day of season. Gillman and staff resign. 

## 1960 Following death of Bert Bell. Pete Rozelle is named NFL commis sioner. Elroy Hirsch replaces Rozelle as Rams general manager. Bob Water-field is named Ram head coach. Team finishes 4-7-1. 

## 1964 Rams sign 10-year pact to play in “new look" Coliseum’s"stadium-within-a-stadium.’’ Fourteen rookies make the season squad. Club finishes fifth with 5-7-2 record. 

## 1965 After winning only one of first 10, Rams take three of last four against' top two teams in each con ference, but Svare is dismissed. 

## 1966 After a court fight, George Allen is released by George Halas from his assistant coaching duties with the Chicago Bears to become head coach of the Rams. NFL and AFL merge in spring. Bob Kelley, 

■'Voice of the Rams" since the club’s beginning in 1937 dies in September. Rams practice in new facilities in Long Beach. Team finishes 8-6. 

## 1967 After 17 years on Beverly Boulevard, club moves to new build ing on Pico. Training camp is also moved to California State College at Fullerton after five years at Chapman College in Orange. Equipment mana ger Bill Gran holm leaves club after 18 years to take position in league office. Rams record first upbeaten presea son in history with six wins, including victories over first-ever AFL oppon ents, San Diego and Kansas City. Team completes finest win-loss sea son ever with 11-1-2 league record to win Coastal Division Championship, the first title of any kind since 1955, then loses to Green Bay in Western Conference Championship Game, 

## 1961 Rams trade Bill Wade, Del Shofner, John Guzik for Zeke Brat-kowski, Lindon Crow and 1962 first draft choice, which makes it possible to draft both Roman Gabriel and Merlin Olsen, Revamped Rams finish strongly after slow start, but still show 4-10-0 deficit. 

## 1962 Harland Svare replaces Don Paul as defensive line coach. Rams lose four of first five games by narrow margins, then show only occasional surges of success en route to 1-12-1 year. Waterfield resigns after eighth game. Svare named interim head coach. On Dec. 27, in closed auction, Reeves reacquires control of Rams, purchasing full interests of co-owners Pauley, Levy, Seley and Bob Hope. 

## 1963 Reeves sells 49% interest in Rams to Gene Autry, Bob Reynolds, Leonard Firestone, Paul A. O'Bryan, Robert Lehman, J.D. Stetson Cole man and Joseph A. Thomas. Svare is retained. Les Richter retires before season. After 0-5 record, Gabriel is reinstated as starting QB and plays last nine games without relief, guid ing team to 5-4 mark and season record of 5-9-0. 

## 1968 After playoff win over Cleve land in January, team finishes regular season with 10-3-1 record, second in Coastal Division to Baltimore's 13-1 mark. Attendance is over one million for second straight year and Ram defense sets new 14-game NFL record 91 for fewest yards allowed- On Dec. 26, Allen is dismissed as head coach, but is re-hired two weeks later. from the estate of the late Dan Reeves. The transaction was completed and announced on July 14. Rosenbloom, the most successful owner in the NFL overthe last two decades, brings with him to Los Angeles Don Klosterman, Rosenbloom's general manager in Baltimore- Klosterman assumes title of Executive Vice President and General Manager. After five years at Cal State Fullerton, Rams move train ing camp site to Cal State Long Beach. After6-7-1 season, all coaches are dismissed. 

## 1969 After 20 years with the Rams as a player, general manager and assistant to the president, Elroy Hirsch leaves club to become athletic director at the University of Wisconsin. He is replaced by Public Relations Director Jack Teele, and John Sanders be comes Assistant General Manager. Team wins its first 11 games to win Coastal Division with 11-3 record before losing to Minnesota in Western Conference title game. 23-20. Quar terback Roman Gabriel is unanimous choice as the NFL's Most Valuable Player. 

## 1973 An observer in 72, Rosen bloom begins to make changes early in 1973. and they pay off quickly. His choice for head coach,former Detroit assistant Chuck Knox, leads team to 12-2 season, winningest in Rams his tory, and Knox becomes "Coach of the Year," Roman Gabriel is traded to Philadelphia and the new quarter back,former San Diego Charger John HadI, is NFC "Player of the Year.” Rams win NFC West title, but lose in first round of playoffs to Dallas. Other changes introduced by Rosenbloom include return to blue and gold uni forms. Club returns to Cal State Ful lerton for summer training. 

## 1970 Playoff Bowl victory over Dallas in January heads Rams toward their 25th year in Southern California. With the completion of the merger of the NFL and AFL, the Rams join San Francisco, Atlanta and New Orleans in the Western Division of the National Conference of the new 26-team National Football League. Rams finish second to 49ers with 9-4-1 record. George Allen’s contract is not renewed. 

## 1971 On April 15, owner Daniel F. Reeves dies of cancer in New York. His longtime friend and business as sociate, William A. Barnes, becomes President and General Manager. Tommy Prothro, successful head coach at UCLA, replaces Allen. Play ing the toughest schedule In the NFL. the Rams finish with an 8-5-1 record, second to 49ers in the NFC West. 

## 1974 Carroll Rosenbloom’s son, Steve, takes over as Assistant to the President. After 3-2 start. Rams trade John HadI to Green Bay for five draft choices in bold move that stuns the football world. Hadl’s backup, James Harris, becomes starter and leads team to 10-4 record,its second straight NFC Western title and its first playoff victory since 1951 (a 19-10 win over Washington) before the Rams bow to Minnesota, 14-10, in NFC title game. 

## 1972 In a history-making move, Baltimore Colts owner Carroll Rosen bloom trades the Baltimore franchise to Robert Irsay in exchange for the Rams. Irsay had purchased the Rams 1975 With defense allowing second fewest points in NFL history over a 92 14-game season (135), Rams win third straight NFC Western title by com pleting 12-2 season. After playoff vic tory over St. Louis, however, they bow to Dallas in the NFC Champion ship Game. The 34-8 record over the last three years is best in the NFL.

Quarterback injuries mar season and rookie Pat Haden becomes fourth different playoff QB in four years under Knox. Rams’351 points is high est in NFC. are together. Despite multitude of injuries, team wins 7th straight division title to set NFL record, then beats Dallas(21-19) and Tampa Bay (9-0) in NFC Playoffs. Rams lose to Pittsburgh in Super Bowl XIV, 31-19. 

# 1980 With Anaheim Stadium’s ca pacity set at 69,045, Rams sell out last six home games and finish with 11-5 record. Rams lead NFL in rushing for first time since 1957, gaining 2,799 yards. Rams set 15 club records and tie three others. Nolan Cromwell named consensus All-NFL and re ceives award as NFC Defensive Player of the Year. Rams enter play offs as wild card and lose to Dallas, 34-13, 

# 1977 Rams spearhead new Coli seum configuration which reduces capacity from 91,038 to 71,039. With Lawrence McCutcheon setting new club career rushing record of 5,523 yards, the Rams (10-4) roll to their fifth straight division title before 14-7 playoff loss to Minnesota in Coliseum. Following the campaign Knox resigns to take Buffalo BINs head coaching post. 

# 1978 On Feb. 1. Rosenbloom hires George Allen but releases Allen after second preseason game, Ray Mala-vasi becomes head coach and leads club to 12-4 mark for the sixth straight division title (tying NFL record). Rams beat Minnesota, 34-10, in playoff but lose NFC title to Dallas. Rams also announce move to Anaheim Stadium beginning in 1980.

10.content:
The NFL signs a five-year contract with the same principles. Total value is estimated to be $2.1 billion. The only noticeable change is that ABC will finally get to cover a Super Bowl. NBC gets Super Bowls XVII and XX, CBS Super Bowls XVIII and XXI, and ABC is to televise Super Bowl XIX.

Also of note, for the first time since 1960, the NFL experiences its first franchise relocation amid much dispute. The Oakland Raiders move to the LA Coliseum and become the Los Angeles Raiders.

One other semi-related item. _USA Today_ begins publishing on September 15. Each Friday in the sports section, the paper presents capsule reports on the weekend's NFL games. Within the capsules are found the network commentator assignments for each NFL game. For the researchers among us, this is a god-send and makes the research for these assignments a lot easier.

When the NFL strike made Milwaukee County Stadium the Packers' home field — in 1982
===================================================================================

 [![Image 1: Portrait of Chris Foran](https://www.jsonline.com/gcdn/presto/2019/10/20/PMJS/198f26ed-b6a0-442a-a6a8-7cb2b4bce95d-MJS_Chris_Foran_-_Employee.jpg?crop=263,263,x114,y20&width=48&height=48&format=pjpg&auto=webp) Chris Foran](https://www.jsonline.com/staff/2648144001/chris-foran/)

Milwaukee Journal Sentinel

Updated Nov. 21, 2017, 11:13 a.m. CT

[](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?display=popup&app_id=227386193957280&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.jsonline.com%2Fstory%2Flife%2Fgreen-sheet%2F2017%2F11%2F21%2Fwhen-nfl-strike-made-milwaukee-county-stadium-packers-home-field-1982%2F874128001%2F)[](https://x.com/intent/post?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.jsonline.com%2Fstory%2Flife%2Fgreen-sheet%2F2017%2F11%2F21%2Fwhen-nfl-strike-made-milwaukee-county-stadium-packers-home-field-1982%2F874128001%2F&text=When%20the%20NFL%20strike%20made%20Milwaukee%20County%20Stadium%20the%20Packers%27%20home%20field%20%E2%80%94%20in%201982&via=journalsentinel)[](mailto:?subject=When%20the%20NFL%20strike%20made%20Milwaukee%20County%20Stadium%20the%20Packers'%20home%20field%20%E2%80%94%20in%201982%20-%20from%20Journal%20Sentinel&body=When%20the%20NFL%20strike%20made%20Milwaukee%20County%20Stadium%20the%20Packers'%20home%20field%20%E2%80%94%20in%201982%0A%0ADuring%20the%201982%20season%2C%20the%20Green%20Bay%20Packers%20played%20more%20games%20in%20Milwaukee%20than%20they%20did%20in%20Green%20Bay.%20You%20could%20look%20it%20up.%0A%0ACheck%20out%20this%20story%20on%20jsonline.com%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.jsonline.com%2Fstory%2Flife%2Fgreen-sheet%2F2017%2F11%2F21%2Fwhen-nfl-strike-made-milwaukee-county-stadium-packers-home-field-1982%2F874128001%2F)

Keep Watching

![Image 2: Running back Gerry Ellis tries to evade tacklers during the Green Bay Packers' 26-7 win over the Minnesota Vikings at County Stadium on Nov. 21, 1982. It was the Packers' first game after the 57-day NFL players strike.](https://www.jsonline.com/gcdn/-mm-/9ad451f9fc7afe6a17a178282ea90a39eb849aec/c=0-275-2587-1737/local/-/media/2017/11/17/WIGroup/Milwaukee/636465211481813312-packers-nov.-21-1982.JPG?width=660&height=373&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

During the 1982 season, the Green Bay Packers played more games in Milwaukee than they did in Green Bay. You could look it up.

On Sept. 21 that year, NFL players went on strike over getting a bigger share of the booming sport's revenue. The strike began two weeks into the season, including the Packers' season-opener at Milwaukee's County Stadium against the Los Angeles Rams (the green and gold won, 35-23).

When the strike ended 57 days later, the Packers started the "second" half of the season at County Stadium, too, on Nov. 21, against the Minnesota Vikings.

![Image 3: Paul Kohorn removes the pitcher's mound at County Stadium, as crews worked on Nov. 17, 1982, to get the field ready for the game between the Green Bay Packers and the Minnesota Vikings. A 57-day strike interrupted the NFL season. This photo was published in the Nov. 18, 1982, Milwaukee Journal.](https://www.jsonline.com/story/life/green-sheet/2017/11/21/when-nfl-strike-made-milwaukee-county-stadium-packers-home-field-1982/874128001/)

How that would go was anyone's guess. As County Stadium crews scrambled to get the field ready, fans weren't exactly doing the Lambeau Leap.

The Sunday before — Nov. 14, two days before the strike ended — The Milwaukee Journal reported that a survey of fans in Milwaukee and Green Bay showed that 65% said they didn't care if the NFL resumed play that season.

Need a news break? [Check out the all new PLAY hub with puzzles, games and more!](https://play.usatoday.com/?itm_source=SPIKE&itm_campaign=PLAYSPIKE&itm_medium=ONSITE)

According to the survey, the Milwaukee Brewers' pennant-winning season had helped ease the pain of losing the Packers. When asked, "If the Milwaukee Brewers had not been in the World Series this fall, would you have missed the Packer games more than you have?" 62% of those surveyed said yes.

The relatively tepid interest in Packers football sparked concerns that not enough tickets would be sold for the Vikings game at County Stadium to prevent the telecast of the game from being blacked out.

Between sluggish demand and tickets returned by disgruntled fans, ticket sellers had about 3,000 tickets left to sell at noon Thursday, Nov. 18 — the deadline for when the team had to decide whether the game would be shown. On Friday, even though the ticket sales were still short, the Packers asked CBS to lift the blackout "in appreciation of the patience Packer fans have shown during the strike," The Journal reported Nov. 19.

For the game on Sunday, an "unenthusiastic" crowd of 44,681 — with 4,799 no-shows and 5,000 unsold tickets, the Milwaukee Sentinel reported on Nov. 22, came to see the Packers thump the Vikings, 26-7.

"We've been in churches that have been louder," William Janz wrote in a front-page column in the Sentinel on Nov. 22. "Maybe Packer fans simply forgot how to cheer during the strike. Maybe so many people stayed home because they thought the game would be as exciting as a New Year's Eve party where only yogurt was served. Maybe it'll take more than three touchdowns and two field goals to offset the hurt brought on many of us by eight weeks of yard work."

RELATED: [Our Back Pages: When Lombardi sacked Milwaukee's bid to land a pro football franchise](https://www.jsonline.com/story/life/green-sheet/2017/10/24/when-lombardi-sacked-milwaukees-bid-land-pro-football-franchise/789376001/)

RELATED: [Our Back Pages: When they had opening day and nobody came](https://www.jsonline.com/story/life/green-sheet/2017/04/11/our-back-pages-when-they-had-opening-day-and-nobody-came/100172978/)

On the field, Vikings coach Bud Grant could tell something was missing: "The enthusiasm wasn't in the ballpark, even with the fans. Maybe because it was deer hunting season," The Journal's Chuck Salituro quoted him as saying in a Nov. 22 column.

Packers offensive tackle Greg Koch put a positive spin on it in the same column: "Today the Packer fans proved to me that they're the best in the world. They showed a lot of class by not booing the players."

The strike had wiped out five games that were to have been played at Lambeau Field that season. The Packers played again at County Stadium on Dec. 5, beating the Buffalo Bills, before traveling to Green Bay to play the team's lone regular-season game at Lambeau — and that turned out to be a 30-10 loss to the Detroit Lions.

"They're mostly the Milwaukee Packers now," New York Times sportswriter Dave Anderson wrote in a story republished in the Nov. 26 Journal.

Powered by their resilient quarterback, Lynn Dickey, and a running game led by Eddie Lee Ivery, the Packers finished the truncated 1982 season 5-3-1.

Thanks to the NFL's rejiggered playoff system, the team returned to Lambeau on Jan. 8, 1983, where they finally won a game in Green Bay, throttling the St. Louis Cardinals, 41-16. (The Packers' postseason ended the following week with a 37-26 loss on the road to the Dallas Cowboys.)

And with the Packers back in winning mode, the fans were back, too.

"My reaction during the strike was I don't give a damn whether they come back," one Milwaukee Packer fan told The Journal's Rich Kirchen in a story on Nov. 22, 1982. "Now I say, 'Look, it's over with, so forget it.' "

Our Back Pages 
---------------

About This Feature 
-------------------

Each Wednesday, Our Back Pages dips into the Journal Sentinel archives, sharing photos and stories from the past that connect, reflect and sometimes contradict the Milwaukee we know today.

Special thanks and kudos go to senior multimedia designer Bill Schulz for finding many of the gems in the Journal Sentinel photo archives.
